s: God makes the world in six days, from light to living creatures, and last of all makes man and woman in his own image. He sees that all of it is very good.
God rests on the seventh day. A closer telling of the first man, placed in the garden of Eden, and of the woman made from his side as his partner.
The serpent tempts Eve and Adam, and they eat the forbidden fruit. Sin, shame and death enter the world, yet God already promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent.
Cain kills his brother Abel out of jealousy and becomes a wanderer. Adam and Eve have another son, Seth, and people begin to call on the Lord.
The family line from Adam to Noah. Enoch walks with God and is taken up, and Methuselah lives longest of all.
People grow so wicked that God regrets making them. Only Noah finds favour, and God tells him to build an ark.
Noah, his family and the animals enter the ark. The flood comes and covers the earth for forty days.
The waters go down and the ark comes to rest. Noah leaves it and offers a sacrifice, and God promises never again to curse the earth this way.
God makes a covenant with Noah and every living thing, with the rainbow as its sign. Noah's son Ham dishonours his father.
The nations of the world descend from Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth.
People build the tower of Babel to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them by confusing their language. The line of Shem leads to Abram.
God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to bless all nations through him. Abram goes to Canaan, then to Egypt in a famine.
Abram and his nephew Lot part ways, Lot choosing the plain near Sodom. God promises Abram the whole land and countless descendants.
Abram rescues Lot from raiding kings. Melchizedek, king and priest of Salem, brings out bread and wine and blesses him.
God promises Abram a son and descendants as many as the stars. Abram believes, and God makes a covenant with him.
Sarai gives her maid Hagar to Abram, and Hagar bears Ishmael. God sees Hagar in the desert and cares for her.
God renames Abram as Abraham and Sarai as Sarah, and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant. He promises that Sarah will bear a son, Isaac.
Three visitors come to Abraham at Mamre and promise Sarah a son within a year. Abraham pleads with God to spare Sodom for the sake of a few just men.
Angels rescue Lot's family before fire destroys Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
In Gerar, Abraham again calls Sarah his sister, and God protects her from King Abimelech.
Isaac is born, as God promised. Hagar and Ishmael are sent away but God provides for them, and Abraham makes a treaty at Beersheba.
God tests Abraham by asking him to offer up Isaac. At the last moment an angel stops him and God provides a ram, renewing his promise.
Sarah dies, and Abraham buys a cave at Machpelah as a family tomb, his first piece of the promised land.
Abraham's servant goes to find a wife for Isaac among his kin and is led by God to Rebekah, who agrees to come.
Abraham dies and is buried beside Sarah. Rebekah bears twins, Esau and Jacob, and Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of stew.
God renews the promise to Isaac. Isaac lives among the Philistines, digs wells and makes peace with Abimelech.
Helped by Rebekah, Jacob disguises himself as Esau and receives Isaac's blessing. Esau vows to kill him.
Jacob is sent away to find a wife. On the way he dreams of a ladder reaching heaven, and God renews the promise to him at Bethel.
Jacob reaches his uncle Laban and loves Rachel, but is tricked into marrying Leah first. Leah bears him four sons.
Rachel and Leah compete in bearing children, and Rachel at last gives birth to Joseph. Jacob grows rich in flocks.
Jacob leaves Laban secretly with his family and herds. Laban chases him, and the two make a covenant of peace.
Jacob prepares to meet Esau. At night he wrestles with a mysterious man, is blessed, and is renamed Israel.
Jacob and Esau are reconciled, and Jacob settles near Shechem.
Dinah is violated at Shechem, and her brothers Simeon and Levi take bloody revenge on the city.
Jacob returns to Bethel and puts away foreign gods. Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac dies.
The descendants of Esau, who becomes the people of Edom.
Jacob favours Joseph, who dreams of ruling his brothers. His jealous brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt.
Judah wrongs his daughter-in-law Tamar, and she bears twins by him, Perez and Zerah.
Joseph serves in Potiphar's house and refuses the advances of his master's wife. Falsely accused, he is thrown into prison, but God is with him.
In prison Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's butler and baker. The butler is restored but forgets him.
Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams of seven good years and seven of famine. Pharaoh makes him ruler over Egypt.
Joseph's brothers come to Egypt to buy grain. He recognizes them, tests them, and keeps Simeon until they bring Benjamin.
The brothers return with Benjamin, and Joseph feasts with them, still hiding who he is.
Joseph's silver cup is hidden in Benjamin's sack. Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.
Joseph reveals himself to his brothers in tears and forgives them, seeing God's hand in all that happened.
God tells Jacob not to fear going down to Egypt. Jacob and his family, seventy people, settle there.
Pharaoh welcomes Jacob's family and gives them Goshen. Joseph manages Egypt through the famine.
Jacob blesses Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, placing the younger before the elder.
Jacob blesses each of his twelve sons before he dies, foretelling that the sceptre will not leave Judah.
Jacob is buried in Canaan. Joseph reassures his brothers that God turned their evil into good, and he dies in Egypt.

1: Everything that exists comes from God. He makes the world out of nothing, and he makes it good.
Human beings are the high point of creation. Every man and woman bears God's image, which is the root of human dignity.
3: Adam and Eve choose their own way over God's command. This first sin, called original sin, brings death and disorder into the world.
The first promise of a Saviour
Right after the Fall, God promises that the woman's offspring will defeat the serpent. Christians call this the first announcement of the Gospel, fulfilled in Christ and Mary.
7: God washes the world clean of its violence but saves Noah's family and the animals in the ark. The Church sees the ark as a picture of baptism and the Church itself.
9: God makes a promise with all creation never again to destroy it by flood. The rainbow is its sign. It is the first of the great covenants.
12: God calls Abram to leave everything and trust him. From this one family God will build a people and, through them, bless all the nations.
14: A mysterious priest-king offers bread and wine and blesses Abram. The Church sees him as a figure of Christ and of the Eucharist.
15: Abram trusts God's promise though he has no son. This faith is counted as righteousness, and Paul later holds it up as the model for every believer.
22: Abraham is ready to give up his only son, and God stops him and provides a ram. It foreshadows God the Father giving his only Son on the cross.
28: Jacob sees heaven opened and angels going up and down. Jesus later says he himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth.
32: After wrestling through the night, Jacob receives a new name, Israel. His twelve sons become the twelve tribes of God's people.
37: Out of jealousy, Joseph's brothers sell him as a slave. God will use even this betrayal to save the whole family.
45: Joseph reveals himself and forgives the brothers who sold him. He sees that God was at work through everything to save lives.
50: Joseph's words sum up the whole story: human sin cannot defeat God's plan. He can bring good even out of evil.

32: Why the sinew is still not eaten

The sinew is what Jewish tradition calls the gid hanasheh, the nerve that runs through the hip and down the thigh, usually identified with the sciatic nerve. In memory of Jacob’s wrestling, Jewish law still forbids eating it in cattle, sheep, goats and other kosher animals; the meat around it is allowed once the nerve and certain fats have been cut out. That cutting, called nikkur, is slow and needs a trained hand, so outside Israel kosher butchers usually sell the whole hindquarter to the ordinary market, and cuts such as sirloin and filet mignon are hard to find as kosher. Hebrew Bibles number this verse 32:33.
